vignette:
Omar, a 22-year-old Middle Eastern man, sat in the therapist's office, his hands tightly clasped in his lap. He was an auditor, a job that required precision and attention to detail, yet lately, every day at work felt like a battle against an unseen enemy. The traumatic event that haunted him occurred last year during a night out with friends. After a few drinks, he had made the mistake of trusting someone he thought he knew. The memory of being assaulted came flooding back whenever he caught a whiff of the cologne that the perpetrator wore, a scent that now felt like a sinister reminder of his vulnerability. This potent reminder drove Omar to avoid places where he might encounter the scent, leading him to isolate himself from gatherings where such triggers could arise. Each time he encountered that familiar cologne, he felt a rush of anxiety that compelled him to withdraw from social situations entirely, believing that staying away was the only way to protect himself from further emotional harm. Even the sight of friends casually discussing their ex-partners would send a chill down his spine, leaving him grappling with feelings of humiliation and self-blame. He often thought to himself, "If only I had been more cautious; someone else wouldn't have gotten into this situation." These negative thoughts cemented his belief that the world was inherently unsafe and that he was incapable of navigating it without taking extreme precautions. Convinced that he could not trust himself to handle any potential danger, Omar began to avoid social gatherings and new experiences, reasoning that if he stayed away, he could prevent more pain and humiliation.

In the months following the assault, Omar found himself developing a set of avoidance strategies that permeated his daily life. He made it a point to stay close to exits, whether he was at work or social gatherings, as if by remaining on the periphery, he could shield himself from potential threats. This need to stay close to exits was fueled by the overwhelming memories of the assault, leaving him feeling that any situation could spiral into danger, compelling him to avoid places where he might feel trapped. By consistently choosing to remain near exits, he reinforced his belief that he was in constant danger, as each act of avoidance seemed to validate his fears and left him feeling more vulnerable than ever. The need to stay close to exits stemmed from the haunting memories of the assault; each time he felt cornered or trapped, it triggered a rush of panic that compelled him to leave the situation entirely, even if it meant missing out on social interactions. In this way, his avoidance of social situations became a rational response to the belief that he was unable to handle potentially dangerous circumstances. His clothing choices also shifted; he began to wear baggy, concealing outfits that masked his body and made him feel less visible. Each time he chose to wear these loose-fitting clothes, he felt a growing sense of shame and a deeper conviction that he was fragile and in need of protection, reinforcing his belief that he must hide from the world. This decision, he reasoned, would help him avoid unwanted attention, but deep down, he felt a growing sense of shame for hiding who he was. Whenever he faced situations where he might be evaluated-like performance reviews or even casual conversations-his anxiety surged. His belief that he would be judged harshly kept him from engaging fully in these situations, leading him to withdraw from interactions, which only deepened his feelings of isolation and inadequacy. Convinced that he would be scrutinized and found wanting, he developed avoidance strategies, steering clear of social interactions altogether, believing it was the only sensible way to cope with the threat of judgment. He feared judgment, convinced that others could see the humiliation etched on his face. This belief that he was constantly scrutinized led him to withdraw further into himself, avoiding eye contact and conversations, as if any engagement might expose his vulnerabilities even more. Omar's heightened sense of threat permeated his thoughts and actions. The constant vigilance he felt made every new experience seem like a potential threat, leading him to avoid even the most benign situations, reinforcing the cycle of fear and avoidance. Having never tested his fears in safe environments, he remained convinced that the world was filled with hidden dangers, and each avoidance strategy only served to heighten his sense of threat. He avoided unfamiliar places, convinced that they held hidden dangers. This constant vigilance made every new experience feel like a potential threat, leading him to withdraw from opportunities that could have brought him joy. Each time he encountered sudden movements in crowded areas, his body would tense up, ready to react, as if bracing for another assault. This constant state of alertness not only affected his physical well-being but also triggered flashbacks to the attack, reinforcing his belief that danger lurked around every corner. Every sensation that felt even remotely alarming heightened his sense of threat, as he began to interpret everyday occurrences-like sudden movements or loud noises-as signs that he was in imminent danger. His avoidance strategies, such as skipping social events or taking long routes to work, only served to remind him of the threat he felt, perpetuating a cycle where he never truly experienced safety in any situation. The more he avoided these experiences, the more he felt that he was living in a world filled with danger, reinforcing his belief that he needed to remain vigilant at all times. His avoidance behaviors, such as skipping social events or taking long routes to work, only further heightened his feelings of threat, as he never allowed himself the opportunity to discover that perhaps these situations weren't as dangerous as he perceived. Each time he chose to avoid a situation that felt threatening, it confirmed for him that he was indeed at risk, solidifying the belief that he could not handle the world outside his self-imposed boundaries. He would often think, "I can't let my guard down; I might end up in the same situation again." This belief pushed him further into a pattern of avoidance, as the more he dodged potential reminders of the assault, the more convinced he became that his fears were justified and that danger was ever-present. This thought perpetuated his cycle of avoidance, as he convinced himself that staying close to exits was not just wise, but necessary for his survival, further deepening his sense of threat. The very strategies he employed to protect himself from perceived threats kept him in a state of heightened anxiety, as he never tested whether the situation was truly dangerous or if he could allow himself to feel safe. Each act of avoidance only served to amplify his sense of threat, as he never had the opportunity to learn that the world was not as dangerous as he believed. By consistently avoiding situations that triggered uncomfortable memories, he inadvertently solidified the belief that those triggers were indeed dangerous, never allowing himself the chance to confront and challenge his fears. This constant feeling of threat made every crowded place feel like a potential trap, reinforcing his belief that he was not safe anywhere, which caused him to steer clear of new experiences. The triggers in his environment intertwined with his maladaptive strategies, creating a cycle that felt inescapable. His avoidance behaviors, while initially comforting, only led to deeper feelings of isolation and misery. The more he concealed himself and the more he steered clear of situations that reminded him of the assault, the more he fell into a pattern of negative self-comparison. His repeated decisions to withdraw only reinforced his belief that he was unworthy of happiness, leading him to feel increasingly less capable of coping with life's challenges. Each time he chose to avoid a social interaction, he felt a deepening conviction that he was weak and fragile, further entrenching his negative self-assessment and belief that he could not handle the world around him. Each time he resorted to avoidance, it confirmed for him that he was weak and incapable, further entrenching his negative self-assessment and sense of failure. Each act of avoidance seemed to reinforce his belief that he was fragile and unable to cope, deepening the sense that he was less worthy than others who moved through life with ease. He often told himself that he used to be a happy person, full of life and aspirations, but now he felt trapped in a shadow of his former self. The more he avoided life, the more deeply entrenched he became in his self-loathing. Omar's world was shrinking, and he could feel the weight of his shame pressing down on him. His friends noticed his withdrawal, but he found it difficult to explain why he felt so different now. The thought that he had become someone who needed to hide away from others confirmed his negative self-assessments, making him feel more isolated and ashamed. He dreaded the idea of opening up, fearing that revealing his trauma would only bring more humiliation. As he sat in the therapist's office, he realized that this cycle of triggers, avoidance, and negative self-assessment was no way to live. He was tired of feeling like a prisoner in his own mind and body. What finally pushed Omar to seek help was a moment of clarity during a particularly difficult week. After a stressful incident at work, where he panicked at a sudden noise and had to leave the room, he understood that he couldn't continue like this. He hoped for a way to reclaim his life, to dismantle the barriers he had built around himself, and to find a path back to the happiness he once knew. Yet, he feared that the very avoidance strategies he relied on to feel safe were also the chains that kept him imprisoned, making it seem as though he could never truly escape the memories that haunted him. Yet, deep down, he feared that the very barriers he built in response to perceived threats would keep him trapped forever, making healing seem almost impossible. But beneath his hope lay a deep fear-what if he could never escape the memories that haunted him? As he sat there, he felt both apprehensive and determined, ready to take the first step toward healing. Every time he felt that sense of danger, it whispered to him that he was fragile and at risk, reinforcing his belief that he must constantly be on guard.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette does not convey how triggers influence Omar's maladaptive strategies.
  e.g. "She stopped taking that route to work entirely — better to add twenty minutes to her commute than to feel that way again."
  e.g. "When the anniversary came around, she kept herself moving all day, cleaning, cooking, anything, because sitting still meant the thoughts would catch up."
  e.g. "She started leaving events early, telling herself she was tired, because staying too long meant the chances of something going wrong only multiplied."
- Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette does not show that negative appraisals lead to maladaptive strategies in Omar's case.
  e.g. "If she had concluded that the world was dangerous and she was defenceless, staying home wasn't avoidance — it was the only rational thing to do."
  e.g. "The belief that speaking about it would make things worse kept her silent in her sessions, offering fragments instead of the whole picture."
  e.g. "Having decided that her feelings couldn't be trusted, she worked hard to stay numb — and had become quite good at it."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals: It is not made clear how maladaptive strategies contribute to negative appraisals in the vignette.
  e.g. "Three years of avoiding it had told her something she couldn't easily argue with: that she must be more fragile than other people, or she would have been over this by now."
  e.g. "Each time she used a safety behaviour to get through the day, she felt the quiet accumulation of evidence that she couldn't cope without it."
  e.g. "The fact that she still needed to do all of this — the checking, the planning, the long way round — confirmed, in some wordless way, that she wasn't getting better."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: The vignette fails to establish that maladaptive strategies lead to further triggers for Omar.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Threat: The connection between maladaptive strategies and a sense of threat is not explicitly stated in the vignette.
  e.g. "Never having stayed in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, her body had never received the evidence it needed — the threat remained as high as the day it was set."
  e.g. "The checking and the avoidance had kept her alive, in her nervous system's accounting, which meant the danger they were responding to must be real and ongoing."
  e.g. "Without ever testing the feeling, she had no way to know that the threat was not what her body insisted it was — the safety behaviours had sealed that possibility off."

vignette_attempts.vignette:
Omar, a 22-year-old Middle Eastern man, sat in the therapist's office, his hands tightly clasped in his lap. He was an auditor, a job that required precision and attention to detail, yet lately, every day at work felt like a battle against an unseen enemy. The traumatic event that haunted him occurred last year during a night out with friends. After a few drinks, he had made the mistake of trusting someone he thought he knew. The memory of being assaulted came flooding back whenever he caught a whiff of the cologne that the perpetrator wore, a scent that now felt like a sinister reminder of his vulnerability. This potent reminder drove Omar to avoid places where he might encounter the scent, leading him to isolate himself from gatherings where such triggers could arise. Even the sight of friends casually discussing their ex-partners would send a chill down his spine, leaving him grappling with feelings of humiliation and self-blame. He often thought to himself, “If only I had been more cautious; someone else wouldn’t have gotten into this situation.” These negative thoughts cemented his belief that the world was inherently unsafe and that he was incapable of navigating it without taking extreme precautions.

In the months following the assault, Omar found himself developing a set of avoidance strategies that permeated his daily life. He made it a point to stay close to exits, whether he was at work or social gatherings, as if by remaining on the periphery, he could shield himself from potential threats. The need to stay close to exits stemmed from the haunting memories of the assault; each time he felt cornered or trapped, it triggered a rush of panic that compelled him to leave the situation entirely, even if it meant missing out on social interactions. In this way, his avoidance of social situations became a rational response to the belief that he was unable to handle potentially dangerous circumstances. His clothing choices also shifted; he began to wear baggy, concealing outfits that masked his body and made him feel less visible. Each time he chose to wear these loose-fitting clothes, he felt a growing sense of shame and a deeper conviction that he was fragile and in need of protection, reinforcing his belief that he must hide from the world. This decision, he reasoned, would help him avoid unwanted attention, but deep down, he felt a growing sense of shame for hiding who he was. Whenever he faced situations where he might be evaluated—like performance reviews or even casual conversations—his anxiety surged. His belief that he would be judged harshly kept him from engaging fully in these situations, leading him to withdraw from interactions, which only deepened his feelings of isolation and inadequacy. He feared judgment, convinced that others could see the humiliation etched on his face. This belief that he was constantly scrutinized led him to withdraw further into himself, avoiding eye contact and conversations, as if any engagement might expose his vulnerabilities even more. Omar’s heightened sense of threat permeated his thoughts and actions. He avoided unfamiliar places, convinced that they held hidden dangers. This constant vigilance made every new experience feel like a potential threat, leading him to withdraw from opportunities that could have brought him joy. Each time he encountered sudden movements in crowded areas, his body would tense up, ready to react, as if bracing for another assault. This constant state of alertness not only affected his physical well-being but also triggered flashbacks to the attack, reinforcing his belief that danger lurked around every corner. His avoidance strategies, such as skipping social events or taking long routes to work, only served to remind him of the threat he felt, perpetuating a cycle where he never truly experienced safety in any situation. The more he avoided these experiences, the more he felt that he was living in a world filled with danger, reinforcing his belief that he needed to remain vigilant at all times. Each time he chose to avoid a situation that felt threatening, it confirmed for him that he was indeed at risk, solidifying the belief that he could not handle the world outside his self-imposed boundaries. He would often think, “I can’t let my guard down; I might end up in the same situation again.” This thought perpetuated his cycle of avoidance, as he convinced himself that staying close to exits was not just wise, but necessary for his survival, further deepening his sense of threat. The very strategies he employed to protect himself from perceived threats kept him in a state of heightened anxiety, as he never tested whether the situation was truly dangerous or if he could allow himself to feel safe. Each act of avoidance only served to amplify his sense of threat, as he never had the opportunity to learn that the world was not as dangerous as he believed. This constant feeling of threat made every crowded place feel like a potential trap, reinforcing his belief that he was not safe anywhere, which caused him to steer clear of new experiences. The triggers in his environment intertwined with his maladaptive strategies, creating a cycle that felt inescapable. His avoidance behaviors, while initially comforting, only led to deeper feelings of isolation and misery. The more he concealed himself and the more he steered clear of situations that reminded him of the assault, the more he fell into a pattern of negative self-comparison. His repeated decisions to withdraw only reinforced his belief that he was unworthy of happiness, leading him to feel increasingly less capable of coping with life’s challenges. Each time he resorted to avoidance, it confirmed for him that he was weak and incapable, further entrenching his negative self-assessment and sense of failure. Each act of avoidance seemed to reinforce his belief that he was fragile and unable to cope, deepening the sense that he was less worthy than others who moved through life with ease. He often told himself that he used to be a happy person, full of life and aspirations, but now he felt trapped in a shadow of his former self. The more he avoided life, the more deeply entrenched he became in his self-loathing. Omar's world was shrinking, and he could feel the weight of his shame pressing down on him. His friends noticed his withdrawal, but he found it difficult to explain why he felt so different now. The thought that he had become someone who needed to hide away from others confirmed his negative self-assessments, making him feel more isolated and ashamed. He dreaded the idea of opening up, fearing that revealing his trauma would only bring more humiliation. As he sat in the therapist's office, he realized that this cycle of triggers, avoidance, and negative self-assessment was no way to live. He was tired of feeling like a prisoner in his own mind and body. What finally pushed Omar to seek help was a moment of clarity during a particularly difficult week. After a stressful incident at work, where he panicked at a sudden noise and had to leave the room, he understood that he couldn't continue like this. He hoped for a way to reclaim his life, to dismantle the barriers he had built around himself, and to find a path back to the happiness he once knew. Yet, deep down, he feared that the very barriers he built in response to perceived threats would keep him trapped forever, making healing seem almost impossible. But beneath his hope lay a deep fear—what if he could never escape the memories that haunted him? As he sat there, he felt both apprehensive and determined, ready to take the first step toward healing. When these moments arose, Omar often found himself retreating from the conversation, convinced that his discomfort was a reflection of his own inadequacy, leading him to avoid social gatherings altogether. Every time he felt that sense of danger, it whispered to him that he was fragile and at risk, reinforcing his belief that he must constantly be on guard.
